claim: The corpus callosum comprises approximately 200 million axons in the human brain.
source: The corpus callosum (CC) is the largest fibre tract in the human brain and comprises approximately 200 million axons (Paul et al., 2007; Tomasch, 1954) connecting similar regions between the left and right cerebral hemispheres (Fenlon and Richards, 2015; Fenlon et al., 2017; Suárez et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Paul et al., 2007 and Tomasch, 1954.

claim: All eutherian mammals have a corpus callosum.
source: All eutherian mammals have a CC (Suárez et al., 2014a; Suarez, 2017; Suárez et al., 2018), with malformations or complete absence (agenesis) of the CC occurring in at least 1 in 4000 human live births (Glass et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Suárez et al., 2014a; Suarez, 2017; Suárez et al., 2018.

claim: Malformations or complete absence (agenesis) of the corpus callosum occur in at least 1 in 4000 human live births.
source: All eutherian mammals have a CC (Suárez et al., 2014a; Suarez, 2017; Suárez et al., 2018), with malformations or complete absence (agenesis) of the CC occurring in at least 1 in 4000 human live births (Glass et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Glass et al., 2008.

claim: Remodelling of the interhemispheric fissure tissue by midline zipper glia is mediated by FGF8 signalling and subsequent regulation of astrogliogenesis by nuclear factor I (NFI) transcription factors.
source: Recently, we demonstrated that remodelling of the IHF tissue by specialized astroglial cells, known as midline zipper glia (MZG; Silver et al., 1993), is mediated by FGF8 signalling and subsequent regulation of astrogliogenesis by nuclear factor I (NFI) transcription factors and is essential to provide a permissive substrate for callosal axons to cross the telencephalic midline (Gobius et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gobius et al., 2016.

claim: Midline zipper glia are derived from radial glia in the telencephalic hinge, located rostral to the third ventricle.
source: MZG are derived from radial glia in the telencephalic hinge, located rostral to the third ventricle.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Midline zipper glia migrate rostro-dorsally as bipolar cells to the interhemispheric fissure pial surface and transition into multipolar astrocytes.
source: From this ventricular zone, they migrate rostro-dorsally as bipolar cells to the IHF pial surface and transition into multipolar astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The transition of midline zipper glia into multipolar astrocytes facilitates their intercalation across the midline and subsequent elimination of the intervening leptomeningeal tissue that comprises the interhemispheric fissure.
source: This latter step facilitates their intercalation across the midline and subsequent elimination of the intervening leptomeningeal tissue that comprises the IHF.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The midline zipper glia fuse the medial septum in a fashion that resembles a 'zipper' mechanism.
source: The MZG thereby fuse the medial septum in a fashion that resembles a 'zipper' mechanism (Gobius et al., 2016), which does not occur in naturally acallosal mammals such as monotremes and marsupials (Gobius et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gobius et al., 2016.

claim: The zipper mechanism does not occur in naturally acallosal mammals such as monotremes and marsupials.
source: The MZG thereby fuse the medial septum in a fashion that resembles a 'zipper' mechanism (Gobius et al., 2016), which does not occur in naturally acallosal mammals such as monotremes and marsupials (Gobius et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gobius et al., 2016.

claim: Developmental defects in interhemispheric fissure remodelling invariably result in callosal agenesis in mouse models.
source: Developmental defects in IHF remodelling invariably result in callosal agenesis in mouse models, and, strikingly, all 38 individuals in a human cohort with callosal agenesis also displayed aberrant retention of the IHF and an abnormal separation of the medial septum (Gobius et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gobius et al., 2016.

claim: All 38 individuals in a human cohort with callosal agenesis displayed aberrant retention of the interhemispheric fissure and an abnormal separation of the medial septum.
source: Developmental defects in IHF remodelling invariably result in callosal agenesis in mouse models, and, strikingly, all 38 individuals in a human cohort with callosal agenesis also displayed aberrant retention of the IHF and an abnormal separation of the medial septum (Gobius et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gobius et al., 2016.

claim: Netrin 1 (NTN1) is a secreted ligand for the deleted in colorectal carcinoma (DCC) receptor.
source: Netrin 1 (NTN1) is a secreted ligand for the deleted in colorectal carcinoma (DCC) receptor, and these molecules function as axon guidance cues in species ranging from Drosophila to mammals (Chan et al., 1996; de la Torre et al., 1997; Fazeli et al., 1997; Hedgecock et al., 1990; Keino-Masu et al., 1996; Kolodziej et al., 1996; Serafini et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: NTN1 and DCC function as axon guidance cues in species ranging from Drosophila to mammals.
source: Netrin 1 (NTN1) is a secreted ligand for the deleted in colorectal carcinoma (DCC) receptor, and these molecules function as axon guidance cues in species ranging from Drosophila to mammals (Chan et al., 1996; de la Torre et al., 1997; Fazeli et al., 1997; Hedgecock et al., 1990; Keino-Masu et al., 1996; Kolodziej et al., 1996; Serafini et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: NTN1-DCC signalling attracts pioneering callosal axons towards the midline.
source: Indeed, NTN1-DCC signalling attracts pioneering callosal axons towards the midline and attenuates chemorepulsive signalling in neocortical callosal axons ex vivo to facilitate crossing the midline (Fothergill et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fothergill et al., 2014.

claim: NTN1-DCC signalling attenuates chemorepulsive signalling in neocortical callosal axons ex vivo to facilitate crossing the midline.
source: Indeed, NTN1-DCC signalling attracts pioneering callosal axons towards the midline and attenuates chemorepulsive signalling in neocortical callosal axons ex vivo to facilitate crossing the midline (Fothergill et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fothergill et al., 2014.

claim: Heterozygous and homozygous DCC pathogenic variants result in human callosal dysgenesis at high frequency.
source: Heterozygous and homozygous DCC pathogenic variants also result in human callosal dysgenesis at high frequency (Jamuar et al., 2017; Marsh et al., 2018; Marsh et al., 2017) with an estimated incidence of 1 in 14 in unrelated individuals with callosal dysgenesis (Marsh et al., 2017), and Ntn1 and Dcc mouse mutants do not form a CC (Fazeli et al., 1997; Finger et al., 2002; Fothergill et al., 2014; Serafini et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jamuar et al., 2017; Marsh et al., 2018; Marsh et al., 2017.

claim: DCC pathogenic variants have an estimated incidence of 1 in 14 in unrelated individuals with callosal dysgenesis.
source: Heterozygous and homozygous DCC pathogenic variants also result in human callosal dysgenesis at high frequency (Jamuar et al., 2017; Marsh et al., 2018; Marsh et al., 2017) with an estimated incidence of 1 in 14 in unrelated individuals with callosal dysgenesis (Marsh et al., 2017), and Ntn1 and Dcc mouse mutants do not form a CC (Fazeli et al., 1997; Finger et al., 2002; Fothergill et al., 2014; Serafini et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marsh et al., 2017.

claim: Ntn1 and Dcc mouse mutants do not form a corpus callosum.
source: Heterozygous and homozygous DCC pathogenic variants also result in human callosal dysgenesis at high frequency (Jamuar et al., 2017; Marsh et al., 2018; Marsh et al., 2017) with an estimated incidence of 1 in 14 in unrelated individuals with callosal dysgenesis (Marsh et al., 2017), and Ntn1 and Dcc mouse mutants do not form a CC (Fazeli et al., 1997; Finger et al., 2002; Fothergill et al., 2014; Serafini et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fazeli et al., 1997; Finger et al., 2002; Fothergill et al., 2014; Serafini et al., 1996.

claim: In Ntn1 and Dcc mutant mice, callosal axons form ipsilateral 'Probst' bundles that run parallel to the midline instead of crossing the midline.
source: Instead of crossing the midline, callosal axons in Ntn1 and Dcc mutant mice form ipsilateral 'Probst' bundles that run parallel to the midline (Fazeli et al., 1997; Finger et al., 2002; Fothergill et al., 2014; Probst, 1901; Ren et al., 2007; Serafini et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In Ntn1 and Dcc mutant mice, only the corpus callosum and hippocampal commissure are completely absent, while other axon tracts remain intact or are mildly affected.
source: However, in Ntn1 and Dcc mutant mice, only the CC and hippocampal commissure (HC) are completely absent, while other axon tracts remain intact or are mildly affected (Fazeli et al., 1997; Serafini et al., 1996; Yung et al., 2015), indicating that additional processes might affect the development of the CC and HC in these mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fazeli et al., 1997; Serafini et al., 1996; Yung et al., 2015.

claim: Elimination of the leptomeninges, which normally occurs during interhemispheric fissure remodelling, is severely disrupted in Ntn1 mutant mice.
source: Moreover, elimination of the leptomeninges, which normally occurs during IHF remodelling (Gobius et al., 2016), is severely disrupted in Ntn1 mutant mice (Hakanen and Salminen, 2015), further suggesting that NTN1 and its receptor, DCC, may play a hitherto unidentified role in IHF tissue remodelling.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gobius et al., 2016 and Hakanen and Salminen, 2015.

claim: NTN1 and DCC signalling play a critical role in regulating astroglial development and interhemispheric fissure remodelling during corpus callosum and hippocampal commissure formation.
source: Here, we identify a distinct and developmentally earlier role for NTN1 and DCC signalling during CC formation, involving the regulation of MZG development and subsequent IHF remodelling.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as a finding of the study.

claim: Interhemispheric fissure remodelling is impaired in both Ntn1 and Dcc mouse mutants.
source: We find that IHF remodelling is impaired in both Ntn1 and Dcc mouse mutants, as well as in humans with DCC pathogenic variants that also display agenesis of the CC and HC.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as a finding of the study.

claim: Humans with DCC pathogenic variants display disrupted interhemispheric fissure remodelling associated with corpus callosum and hippocampal commissure malformations.
source: We find that IHF remodelling is impaired in both Ntn1 and Dcc mouse mutants, as well as in humans with DCC pathogenic variants that also display agenesis of the CC and HC.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as a finding of the study.

claim: Human pathogenic variants of DCC are unable to regulate cell morphology, in contrast to the wildtype receptor.
source: Moreover, in contrast to the wildtype receptor, these human pathogenic variants of DCC are unable to regulate cell morphology.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as a finding of the study.

claim: Defects in astroglial morphology and migration to the interhemispheric fissure in Ntn1 and Dcc mutant mice prevent midline zipper glia intercalation and interhemispheric fissure remodelling.
source: Furthermore, we find that defects in astroglial morphology and migration to the IHF in Ntn1 and Dcc mutant mice prevent MZG intercalation and, therefore, IHF remodelling and midline crossing of commissural axons.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as a finding of the study.

claim: Pathogenic variants in NTN1 and DCC are most likely to affect human corpus callosum and hippocampal commissure development through misregulation of astroglial shape, motility and function during interhemispheric fissure remodelling.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that pathogenic variants in NTN1 and DCC are most likely to affect human CC and HC development through misregulation of astroglial shape, motility and function during IHF remodelling.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as a conclusion of the study.

claim: Commissural axons in Dcc knockout, Dcckanga, and Ntn1-lacZ mice remain within the ipsilateral hemisphere and do not form a corpus callosum or hippocampal commissure.
source: This revealed that commissural axons in Dcc knockout, Dcckanga, and Ntn1-lacZ mice remain within the ipsilateral hemisphere and do not form a CC or HC, consistent with previous reports (Fazeli et al., 1997; Finger et al., 2002; Fothergill et al., 2014; Ren et al., 2007; Serafini et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in the manuscript and citations to previous reports.

claim: Interhemispheric fissure remodelling had not occurred in Dcc knockout, Dcckanga, and Ntn1-lacZ mice, evidenced by complete retention of the interhemispheric fissure.
source: We further identified that IHF remodelling had not occurred in Dcc knockout, Dcckanga, and Ntn1-lacZ mice, evidenced by complete retention of the IHF, which separated the majority of the telencephalic midline (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The extent of interhemispheric fissure retention is significantly larger in Dcc and Ntn1 mutants compared to their wildtype littermates.
source: The extent of IHF retention, measured as the ratio of IHF length to total midline length, is significantly larger in Dcc and Ntn1 mutants compared to their wildtype littermates (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1A, B), but did not differ between mutants (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A, B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The extent of interhemispheric fissure retention did not differ between Dcc and Ntn1 mutants.
source: The extent of IHF retention, measured as the ratio of IHF length to total midline length, is significantly larger in Dcc and Ntn1 mutants compared to their wildtype littermates (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1A, B), but did not differ between mutants (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A, B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The retention of the interhemispheric fissure and absence of the corpus callosum and hippocampal commissure persists into adulthood in Dcckanga mice.
source: However, immunohistochemistry for the axonal marker neurofilament in adult Dcckanga mice revealed that the retention of the IHF and absence of the CC and HC persists into adulthood (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), resembling human congenital callosal agenesis (Edwards et al., 2014; Gobius et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Four individuals from two unrelated families carrying missense pathogenic variants in DCC all displayed complete absence of the corpus callosum associated with aberrant retention of the interhemispheric fissure and an unfused septum.
source: T1-weighted MRI of four individuals from two unrelated families carrying missense pathogenic variants in DCC (p.Val793Gly affecting fibronectin type III-like domain 4 of DCC and p.Met1217Val; p.Ala1250Thr affecting the cytoplasmic domain of DCC; Figure 8A; Marsh et al., 2017) revealed in all cases that the complete absence of the CC was associated with aberrant retention of the IHF and an unfused septum (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 8A.

claim: Individuals with DCC mutations were previously reported to lack a hippocampal commissure.
source: Importantly, these individuals were also previously reported to lack a HC (Marsh et al., 2017), suggesting that a defect in IHF remodelling may also impact HC development.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marsh et al., 2017.

claim: DCC is expressed on axons of the corpus callosum, hippocampal commissure and the fornix during midline development.
source: We previously demonstrated that DCC is expressed on axons of the CC, HC and the fornix during midline development, while NTN1 is expressed at the telencephalic midline, within the indusium griseum and the septum but not within callosal axons themselves (Fothergill et al., 2014; Shu et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fothergill et al., 2014 and Shu et al., 2000.

claim: NTN1 is expressed at the telencephalic midline, within the indusium griseum and the septum but not within callosal axons themselves during midline development.
source: We previously demonstrated that DCC is expressed on axons of the CC, HC and the fornix during midline development, while NTN1 is expressed at the telencephalic midline, within the indusium griseum and the septum but not within callosal axons themselves (Fothergill et al., 2014; Shu et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fothergill et al., 2014 and Shu et al., 2000.

claim: Dcc and Ntn1 are expressed by midline zipper glia (MZG).
source: Fluorescent in situ hybridization for Dcc and Ntn1 transcripts, combined with immunohistochemistry for the MZG marker Glast (Gobius et al., 2016), revealed Dcc and Ntn1 expression in radial MZG progenitor cells within the telencephalic hinge at E12 and E15 (Figure 2B–D, F, H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–J), and in MZG migrating to the IHF at E15 (Figure 2F, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B–D, F, H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–J.

claim: Dcc is expressed in Glast-positive radial glia within the septum but not in the neocortex.
source: Furthermore, Dcc was expressed in Glast-positive radial glia within the septum but not in the neocortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: DCC protein can be identified on Glast-positive processes of radial glia attached to the interhemispheric fissure.
source: DCC protein can be identified on Glast-positive processes of radial glia attached to the IHF (Figure 2G), which are adjacent to Gap43-positive axons traversing the midline region that also express DCC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Following interhemispheric fissure remodelling at E17, mature Gfap-positive/Sox9-positive multipolar MZG cells and Glast-positive MZG cells within the telencephalic hinge continue to express DCC.
source: Following IHF remodelling at E17, mature Gfap-positive/Sox9-positive multipolar MZG cells (Gobius et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2017) and Glast-positive MZG cells within the telencephalic hinge continue to express DCC (Figure 2J–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2J–L.

claim: NTN1 protein is present on the interhemispheric fissure basement membrane, on growing commissural axons and on MZG membranes in control heterozygotes, but not in Ntn1-lacZ homozygous mutant mice.
source: Furthermore, we identified NTN1 protein on the IHF basement membrane (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), on growing commissural axons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G) and on MZG membranes in control heterozygotes, but not in Ntn1-lacZ homozygous mutant mice (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: MZG cells produce and secrete NTN1 that becomes deposited on the basement membrane of the interhemispheric fissure, on commissural axons and on MZG cell processes in the region of initial interhemispheric fissure remodelling.
source: Therefore, MZG cells produce and secrete NTN1 that becomes deposited on the basement membrane of the IHF, on commissural axons and on MZG cell processes in the region of initial IHF remodelling (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Distinct differences in MZG development in Dcckanga mice are observed from E14 onwards, but not in radial MZG progenitors at E13.
source: Immunohistochemistry for Nestin and Glast, which are markers of radial MZG, revealed distinct differences in MZG development in Dcckanga mice from E14 onwards, but not in radial MZG progenitors at E13 (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In wildtype mice, the endfeet and cell bodies of radial Glast-positive MZG cells are evenly distributed along the medial septum and adjacent to the pial surface of the interhemispheric fissure.
source: In wildtype mice, the endfeet and cell bodies of radial Glast-positive MZG cells are evenly distributed along the medial septum and adjacent to the pial surface of the IHF (Figure 3B, D, Figure 4A, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, D and Figure 4A, C.

claim: In Dcckanga mutants, radial MZG accumulate at the base of the interhemispheric fissure.
source: However, in Dcckanga mutants, radial MZG accumulate at the base of the IHF (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A–D.

claim: Long radial Nestin-positive MZG processes extending from the ventricular zone to the rostral-most pial surface of the interhemispheric fissure are noticeably absent from Dcckanga mutants.
source: Furthermore, long radial Nestin-positive MZG processes extending from the ventricular zone to the rostral-most pial surface of the IHF are noticeably absent from Dcckanga mutants, and instead, Nestin-positive Dcckanga processes cluster close to the rostral IHF pial surface and appear disorganized (Figure 3A, C, C', E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, C, C', E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: There is a significant increase in fluorescence intensity of Glast staining within the base of the interhemispheric fissure and a concomitant decrease in the region 150–200 µm distant from the interhemispheric fissure base in Dcckanga mutants compared to their wildtype littermates at E14.
source: These abnormalities were further quantified as a significant increase in fluorescence intensity of Glast staining within the base of the IHF and a concomitant decrease in the region 150–200 µm distant from the IHF base in Dcckanga mutants compared to their wildtype littermates at E14 (Supplementary file 1; Figure 3B, B', G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, B', G and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Just prior to interhemispheric fissure remodelling at E15, there was an overall decrease in Glast-positive radial MZG processes in Dcckanga mutants.
source: Just prior to IHF remodelling at E15, there was an overall decrease in Glast-positive radial MZG processes in Dcckanga mutants (Figure 3C, H; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C, H and Supplementary file 1.

claim: A similar defect in the distribution of Glast-positive MZG processes was identified in Ntn1-lacZ mutant mice at E15.
source: Interestingly, we identified a similar defect in the distribution of Glast-positive MZG processes in Ntn1-lacZ mutant mice at E15 (Figure 3K).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The distribution of Nestin-positive and Glast-positive MZG along the interhemispheric fissure was significantly decreased at both E14 and E15 in Dcckanga mice compared to their wildtype littermates.
source: The distribution of Nestin-positive and Glast-positive MZG along the IHF was significantly decreased at both E14 and E15 in Dcckanga mice compared to their wildtype littermates (Figure 3A–D, J; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A–D, J and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The attachment of MZG processes to the interhemispheric fissure pial surface is specifically reduced in the rostral region of the interhemispheric fissure prior to interhemispheric fissure remodelling in Dcckanga mice.
source: The attachment of MZG processes to the IHF pial surface is therefore specifically reduced in the rostral region of the IHF prior to IHF remodelling in Dcckanga mice.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as an interpretation of the data.

claim: There was no difference in fluorescence intensity of Nestin-positive MZG processes within 5 µm adjacent to the interhemispheric fissure surface between Dcckanga and wildtype mice.
source: There was no difference in fluorescence intensity of Nestin-positive MZG processes within 5 µm adjacent to the IHF surface between Dcckanga and wildtype mice, suggesting comparable attachment of radial glial endfeet to the IHF in both strains (Supplementary file 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, G and Supplementary file 1.

claim: α- and β-dystroglycan are normally localized at the pial interhemispheric fissure surface in Dcckanga mice.
source: This was further evidenced by the normal localization of α- and β-dystroglycan at the pial IHF surface in Dcckanga mice, where these molecules form crucial adhesions between radial glial endfeet and the extracellular matrix (Myshrall et al., 2012; Supplementary file 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: β-catenin and N-cadherin were expressed normally within Dcckanga Nestin-positive radial glia.
source: Moreover, molecules that normally maintain the bipolar morphology of radial glia, such as β-catenin and N-cadherin, were also expressed normally within Dcckanga Nestin-positive radial glia, but adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) was instead significantly reduced in Dcckanga Nestin-positive radial glial endfeet (Supplementary file 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E; Yokota et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) was significantly reduced in Dcckanga Nestin-positive radial glial endfeet.
source: Moreover, molecules that normally maintain the bipolar morphology of radial glia, such as β-catenin and N-cadherin, were also expressed normally within Dcckanga Nestin-positive radial glia, but adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) was instead significantly reduced in Dcckanga Nestin-positive radial glial endfeet (Supplementary file 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E; Yokota et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E and Supplementary file 1.

claim: APC regulates the growth and extension of basal radial glial processes and cell polarity of radial glia and migrating astrocytes.
source: APC regulates the growth and extension of basal radial glial processes and cell polarity of radial glia and migrating astrocytes (Etienne-Manneville and Hall, 2003; Yokota et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Etienne-Manneville and Hall, 2003 and Yokota et al., 2009.

claim: Dcckanga mice showed reduced somal translocation to the interhemispheric fissure.
source: In contrast, Dcckanga mice showed reduced somal translocation to the IHF (Supplementary file 1; Figure 4A, C, G), with significantly fewer MZG cells at the IHF pial surface by E15 in Dcckanga compared to wildtype mice (Supplementary file 1; Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A, C, G and Supplementary file 1.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the number of cell bodies reaching the rostral interhemispheric fissure pial surface in E15 Dcckanga mice.
source: When binned along the rostro-caudal axis, we found a significant reduction in the number of cell bodies reaching the rostral IHF pial surface in E15 Dcckanga mice (200–250 µm; Supplementary file 1; Figure 4C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C, D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: There was a significant increase in MZG cell bodies present at the interhemispheric fissure pial surface between E15 and E16 in Dcckanga mice.
source: There was, however, a significant increase in MZG cell bodies present at the IHF pial surface between E15 and E16 in Dcckanga mice (Supplementary file 1; Figure 4C, E, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C, E, G and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Cell birth-dating, differentiation and apoptosis experiments did not reveal any significant differences between the MZG of Dcckanga and wildtype mice.
source: Furthermore, despite DCC having been previously implicated in regulating cell proliferation and cell death (Arakawa, 2004; Llambi et al., 2001; Mehlen et al., 1998), cell birth-dating, differentiation and apoptosis experiments did not reveal any significant differences between the MZG of Dcckanga and wildtype mice (Supplementary file 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: In Dcckanga and Dcc knockout mice, the glial wedge was malformed and there was a major reduction in somal translocation of Sox9-positive indusium griseum glia to the interhemispheric fissure surface.
source: In Dcckanga and Dcc knockout mice, the glial wedge was malformed and there was a major reduction in somal translocation of Sox9-positive indusium griseum glia to the IHF surface, which subsequently prevented formation of this glial guidepost cell population (Supplementary file 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Members of the FGF8-MAPK-NFI signalling pathway (Fgf8, NFIA, NFIB and p-ERK1/2) were expressed normally in Dcckanga MZG compared to MZG in their wildtype littermates at E15.
source: Members of this signalling pathway (Fgf8, NFIA, NFIB and p-ERK1/2) were expressed normally in Dcckanga MZG compared to MZG in their wildtype littermates at E15 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, D–F; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, D–F and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Dcckanga MZG continue to express Mmp2 mRNA.
source: Further, Dcckanga MZG continue to express Mmp2 mRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D; Supplementary file 1), which we previously demonstrated to be expressed during MZG-mediated degradation of the IHF during remodelling (Gobius et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Ntn1-lacZ, Dcckanga and Dcc knockout MZG remain attached to the caudal interhemispheric fissure pial surface and have not intercalated at stages equivalent to when wildtype MZG have infiltrated and remodelled the interhemispheric fissure.
source: Immunohistochemistry for Nestin, Glast (Figure 3F, J) and Gfap (Figure 5A) demonstrated that Dcckanga, Dcc knockout and Ntn1-lacZ MZG remain attached to the caudal IHF pial surface and have not intercalated at stages equivalent to when wildtype MZG have infiltrated and remodelled the IHF (Figure 3F, K, Figure 5A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F, K, Figure 5A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: DCC-deficient MZG expressed GFAP at comparable levels to wildtype MZG at E17 and demonstrated no precocious expression of GFAP at E15.
source: DCC-deficient MZG expressed GFAP at comparable levels to wildtype MZG at E17 and demonstrated no precocious expression of GFAP at E15, similar to wildtype MZG (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Ntn1-lacZ, Dcckanga and Dcc knockout mice demonstrate a significant reduction of GFAP-positive glia at E17 in the region where the corpus callosum normally forms in wildtype mice.
source: However, Ntn1-lacZ, Dcckanga and Dcc knockout mice demonstrate a significant reduction of GFAP-positive glia at E17 in the region where the CC normally forms in wildtype mice (i.e., >450 µm from the third ventricle; Figure 5A–C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A–C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the rostro-caudal ratio of GFAP fluorescence in Ntn1-lacZ, Dcckanga and Dcc knockout mice compared to controls.
source: We observed a significant reduction in the rostro-caudal ratio of GFAP fluorescence in Ntn1-lacZ, Dcckanga and Dcc knockout mice compared to controls (Figure 5A–D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A–D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: At birth, a spectrum of callosal phenotypes was observed in Dcc cKO mice, including complete callosal absence (4/12 mice), partial CC absence (5/12 mice) and a normal CC that was comparable to control mice (3/12 mice).
source: At birth, we observed a spectrum of callosal phenotypes in Dcc cKO mice, including complete callosal absence (4/12 mice), partial CC absence (5/12 mice) and a normal CC that was comparable to control mice, which do not express Emx1iCre (3/12 mice) based on rostral-caudal CC length across ventral, middle and dorsal horizontal sections (Figure 6A, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A, F.

claim: The hippocampal commissure was significantly reduced in the majority of Dcc cKO animals and was absent in one Dcc cKO mouse.
source: Moreover, the HC was significantly reduced in the majority of animals and was absent in one Dcc cKO mouse (Figure 6A, H; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A, H and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The interhemispheric fissure was significantly retained across Dcc cKO mice, indicating that interhemispheric fissure remodelling had not been completed.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that the IHF was significantly retained across Dcc cKO mice, indicating that IHF remodelling had not been completed (Figure 6A, D–E; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A, D–E and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The severity of callosal agenesis and hippocampal commissure dysgenesis was significantly correlated with the extent to which the interhemispheric fissure had been remodelled in Dcc cKO mice.
source: The severity of callosal agenesis and HC dysgenesis was significantly correlated with the extent to which the IHF had been remodelled (Figure 6A, J, K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–G; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A, J, K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–G and Supplementary file 1.

claim: DCC expression was significantly reduced in the cingulate cortex and adjacent intermediate zone in the majority of P0 Dcc cKO mice.
source: We found that DCC expression was significantly reduced in the cingulate cortex and adjacent intermediate zone in the majority of P0 Dcc cKO mice (mean expression reduced to 80.4 and 62.9%, respectively; Figure 6A, I; Supplementary file 1), and within E15 Dcc cKO mice (mean DCC expression in the cingulate cortex reduced to 76.6% in Dcc cKO; Figure 6L, O; Supplementary file 1), as expected.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A, I, L, O and Supplementary file 1.

claim: TDTOMATO-positive/GAP43-positive axons, which had reduced DCC expression, approached the interhemispheric midline in Dcc cKO mice, similar to their cre-negative littermates.
source: Surprisingly, we found that TDTOMATO-positive/GAP43-positive axons, which had reduced DCC expression, approached the interhemispheric midline in Dcc cKO mice, similar to their cre-negative littermates (Figure 6M–N, P; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6M–N, P and Supplementary file 1.

claim: TDTOMATO-positive/GLAST-positive MZG cell bodies were observed within the telencephalic hinge and at the interhemispheric fissure surface in Dcc cKO mice.
source: Mean DCC expression within the telencephalic hinge was comparable between Dcc cKO mice and their cre littermates (Figure 6L, O; Supplementary file 1), but we also observed TDTOMATO-positive/GLAST-positive MZG cell bodies within the telencephalic hinge, and at the IHF surface in Dcc cKO mice (Figure 6Q–R; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6L, O, Q–R and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Expression of DCC:TDTOMATO in U251 cells in the absence of ligand promoted cell spreading and elongation, reflected by a significant increase in average cell area and cell perimeter, and a significant decrease in cell circularity compared to control.
source: Expression of DCC:TDTOMATO in U251 cells in the absence of ligand (vehicle alone) promoted cell spreading and elongation, reflected by a significant increase in average cell area and cell perimeter, and a significant decrease in cell circularity compared to control (Supplementary file 1; Figure 7A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A–F and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The morphological changes induced by DCC expression were not observed following expression of the DCCkanga construct alone.
source: This effect was not observed following expression of the DCCkanga construct alone (Supplementary file 1; Figure 7A–F), suggesting that the P3 domain of DCC is critical for inducing changes in glial cell shape.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A–F and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The P3 domain of DCC is critical for inducing changes in glial cell shape.
source: This effect was not observed following expression of the DCCkanga construct alone (Supplementary file 1; Figure 7A–F), suggesting that the P3 domain of DCC is critical for inducing changes in glial cell shape.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the data shown in Figure 7A–F and Supplementary file 1.

claim: A similar effect of DCC overexpression on cell morphology was observed in N2A cells, which also registered a significant increase in average cell area and cell perimeter, and decrease in cell circularity, compared to controls.
source: A similar effect was observed following DCC overexpression in N2A cells, which also registered a significant increase in average cell area and cell perimeter, and decrease in cell circularity, compared to controls (Supplementary file 1; Figure 7G–I, Figure 7—figure supplement 1G, H), further indicating similar effects on cell morphology in glial and neural progenitor lineages.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7G–I, Figure 7—figure supplement 1G, H and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Application of NTN1 did not affect cell shape following DCC expression in either U251 or N2A cell lines.
source: Interestingly, application of NTN1 did not affect cell shape following DCC expression in either cell line (Supplementary file 1; Figure 7A–F), suggesting that endogenous NTN1, which is known to be expressed by U251 cells (Chen et al., 2013), may be sufficient for activation of DCC:TDTOMATO receptors or that NTN1 is not required for this effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A–F and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Both U251 and N2A cell lines expressed NTN1 endogenously.
source: We confirmed that both our cell lines expressed NTN1 endogenously and that transfection of DCC increased DCC levels but did not affect NTN1 expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1J.

claim: No endogenous DCC was detected by western blot in either U251 or N2A cell lines.
source: No endogenous DCC was detected by western blot in either cell line (Figure 7—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1J.

claim: No difference in cleaved-caspase 3-mediated cell apoptosis was observed following DCC expression in either U251 or N2A cell lines.
source: No difference in cleaved-caspase 3-mediated cell apoptosis was observed following DCC expression in either cell line (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1I.

claim: DCC mutant proteins with altered residues located at the NTN1 binding interface (p.V793G and p.G805E) were unable to bind NTN1.
source: Using a previously established in vitro binding assay (Müller and Soares, 2006; Zelina et al., 2014), we discovered that DCC mutant proteins with altered residues located at the NTN1 binding interface (p.V793G and p.G805E) were unable to bind NTN1 (Figure 8B), while all other receptors with altered residues lying outside of the NTN1 binding interface still bound NTN1 (p.M743L, p.V754M, p.A893T and p.M1217;A1250T; Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: All other DCC mutant receptors with altered residues lying outside of the NTN1 binding interface still bound NTN1 (p.M743L, p.V754M, p.A893T and p.M1217;A1250T).
source: Using a previously established in vitro binding assay (Müller and Soares, 2006; Zelina et al., 2014), we discovered that DCC mutant proteins with altered residues located at the NTN1 binding interface (p.V793G and p.G805E) were unable to bind NTN1 (Figure 8B), while all other receptors with altered residues lying outside of the NTN1 binding interface still bound NTN1 (p.M743L, p.V754M, p.A893T and p.M1217;A1250T; Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: All eight mutant DCC receptors were unable to modulate cell morphology in the presence of NTN1.
source: Surprisingly, all eight mutant DCC receptors were unable to modulate cell morphology in the presence of NTN1 (Figure 8C–E; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C–E and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Axon guidance molecules such as DCC and NTN1 first regulate the formation of a midline substrate for dorsal commissures prior to their role in regulating axonal growth and guidance across it.
source: Thus, axon guidance molecules such as DCC and NTN1 first regulate the formation of a midline substrate for dorsal commissures prior to their role in regulating axonal growth and guidance across it.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the abstract as a conclusion of the study.
